content_html:
From a recent article in The Economist. It turns out that once again many of the jobs that people predicted would be eliminated by AI have instead received a boost, at least for now. This closely follows another recent report on how Indian BPO firms are surprisingly thriving due to AI.

"Moreover, AI is helping offshore workers in the Philippines do new, more complex jobs. They are picking up work training AI models or supervising AI agents. Hospitals in America are increasingly outsourcing the checking of insurance eligibility and filing of medical records to Filipinos packing AI tools. Mr Gallimore says more “high-value” work, such as accountancy or engineering, is going offshore in part because “AI is a leveller. You can now teach someone complex stuff quickly” and still get it done more cheaply than in America or Europe. Some of this is done at so-called global capability centres, captive back offices that are booming in India and also now growing in the Philippines."

It seems like AI has incidentally commoditized the complement (procedural knowledge), and in turn created greater demand for inputs like human judgement and "empathy".


> It seems like AI has incidentally commoditized the complement (procedural knowledge), and in turn created greater demand for inputs like human judgement and "empathy".

I think as well there is currently the following: AI still needs an operator, in the same way than a bulldozer needs a bulldozer operator. And like with bulldozer, there are always something that business stakeholder wanna dig, now that digging is faster.


“Hospitals in America are increasingly outsourcing the checking of insurance eligibility and filing of medical records to Filipinos packing AI tools. Mr Gallimore says”

How is this HIPPA compliant? Please tell me there’s an aspect of HIPPA that requires sensitive data to be only accessed and processed by Americans on shore. You’d think the multiples we pay on health care for worse outcomes would at least be supporting our own domestic middle class with this sort of basic back office white collar work


This is already common for both HIPAA and financial data, it usually comes down to the offshoring site meeting compliance guidelines and functioning like a "clean room" with data leak prevention in place

Also though, I don't think there is anything inherently less secure about a Filipino handling my data than an America


I visited India recently and when I saw just how many companies have a GCC there I was mindblown. Lots of cool offices, engineering and technical roles, great work life balance and generally a different vibe. Literally every company that I could recognise had a back office there.


Do these GCC's have great work life balance? They may be better that the service companies, and may pay better, but WLB is shitty everywhere in India as far as I can tell. As an example, the death of Ernest & Young employee Anna Sebastian sparked a lot of discussion in Indian media since it was attributed to work pressure.[1] Another example I recently heard was a USA Texas based company called CorroHealth suddenly closing shop and laying off 800+ employees in India, the employees allege it was retaliation for asking for overtime payment since they were being made to work till 10 pm.[2]

If you are an American or European with colleagues in India, and if they are working or attending meetings after regular work hours, they don't have good WLB. Given a choice, I doubt they would want to attend the late night meetings. Life in India is already like playing a video game in hard mode, and yet we have to work lot more hours for lot less pay, and be regularly told how shitty offshoring work is.

[1]https://www.news18.com/viral/26-year-old-ey-pune-employee-su...

[2]https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/tamil-nadu/it-employe...


> but WLB is shitty everywhere in India as far as I can tell

This was what I believed, then I saw how pretty much ALL of my friends at Fortune 100s or 500s and they were amazing. I am sure awful companies exist and the bar for what is good WLB can be lowered by these, but the whole "it is bad everywhere" was simply not true and I felt I had a distorted vision of my Indian friends until I actually visited a lot of them.

My so works at a reinsurance company in one of these GCCs, and her WLB is unmatched. Hours are really flexible. Has a really great manager and team. She even gets to take a day off every month as menstrual leave.

> work lot more hours for lot less pay,

This depends, while the vast majority of roles pay "market rate" there is a strange sweet spot where roles pay a significant amount considering purchasing power and cost of living.


WLB is truly awful in India. People are stretched and stressed out at work, in addition to awful civic conditions which makes travelling to and from work a nightmare. I am not sure how long this can continue.


It does depend on the company and your role. Working a senior role at a FAANG in India is much nicer than junior roles in the local WITCHes (Wipro Infosys etc), which are notorious for their crap salaries and shitty labour practices.


Please don't take me wrong, but FAANG is like not even 0.00001% of Indian labour. Outside of may be the FAANG (have doubts about Amazon), pretty much all companies are bad, even the American or European GCCs don't seem to be good. Note that I am not thinking just about IT - banks, police all seem to have terrible work cultures.


Will we have good civic sense, streets and road culture before we get old? I can only hope.

From https://theprint.in/opinion/indias-poor-little-rich-people/2...

"The purpose of life of an Indian is to escape India, it can either be done by leaving India physically or figuratively by shifting to a gated community. Once the Indian escapes India, India becomes the best country in the world & requires no improvement".

"By walling themselves away, India’s rich secede from society. If the elites don’t use public services, there is less pressure on the state to improve them."


I presume they organized some cringe dances and cultural programme when GP visited, which might have led the GP to conclude that these people live great WLB.


Global capability centers where they basically do the business processes and work for US/EU companies for fraction the cost.


BPO means the US company is outsourcing to an Indian company. A Global Capability Center (GCC) means it's a US company subsidiary in India.


Aka an office or a department in another location where payrates are less than the company median. Coming up with these initialisms must be hard work, I doubt AI is that clever.


> so-called global capability centres, captive back offices that are booming in India ...


We have moved some "low cost" work from India to other reigons, now that translation is improved...

At the same time, we are reducing the proportion of outsourced work, because a local team with LLMs are dramatically more capable... There so many benefits to how you can organize a smaller high-skill team. I would put a 10-man team with the current tooling on par with a 10 high skill + 80 low cost heads even 5 years ago.


Yeah, paradoxically Indian software outsourcing is growing. I guess the way the companies are thinking about this is we need some sort of human oversight for all the work the LLMs are doing, might as well pay someone the least amount possible to do that.


Don't understand why this should not have been obvious. If you have technology that allows expensive workers to do things cheaper why wouldn't same technology allow cheaper workers to do stuff even cheaper... And cheap is good...


Cheaper price doesn't always lead to as large increase in demand. There is only so much writing and translation that is needed. So lowering price does not mean that same amount or more money is spend.

On other hand companies getting these services cheaper can mean that they have less pressure to increase prices.

I think whole Jevon's paradox is misapplied. More efficient use of coal leads to more use cases as they become profitable. Which there was lot of. With many other things like writing or translation there might not be more use cases.


I know a freelance translator and they have more business than ever, AI being "mostly" right is not good enough in many businesses. You need oversight and most importantly - accountability in the form of a human that can put their stamp of approval.


Indian tech sector has seen rapid decline; the Indian outsourcing model is obsolete.

I can now translate tasks that can be easily split to low cost regions, and not have to deal with the cultural issues of India. I can also rapidly generate work of similar (and improving) quality... I have no use for a meat-proxy to a llm.

I expect a severe crash in the Indian tech sector, before a minute proportion of the workers can start to build it up again.


I’m not sure if this is true. I really want the hiring story to be true, but the responses I am getting from people on the ground vs industry generated reports isn’t meeting up.

The only report that I know of that is available is the ICRIER report.

I haven’t read the report itself, but it’s supposed to show modest hiring growth.

Conversely I know that most of the outsourcing vendors are seeing reductions in headcount when it comes to outsourced tech operations.


> Hospitals in America are increasingly outsourcing the checking of insurance eligibility and filing of medical records to Filipinos packing AI tools

So, insurance claims are handled by people who operate in different legal system and by unaccountable undererministic system. And people are pressured to perform fast.

This is not about "automating complex task". This is about "create accountability sink for fraud we want them to do and create system that will perform said fraud".


The insurance company is still liable in US courts for products or services sold in the US, just like any other business is liable regardless of where or who does the work.

Also, pretty sure denial of coverage letters have to be endorsed by US licensed doctors and pharmacists, at least in any half decent state.


Ooph, now the AI will be wrong and the human won't know it. And that's running our... let me see... life saving care. Cool. cool. cool.


"Computer says no" is about unhelpful bureaucracy. Being knowingly locked to a specific procedure and unwilling to divert from it is a different thing from mistakes being made that you are blissfully unaware of. The problem is now invisible and the patient is dying for no reason anyone can discern.


The "unhelpful bureaucracy" arises precisely because the process is structured so there's no point in the chain that can actually consider and solve your problem directly. The process is the point, outsourcing work to the opposite end of the globe has long been a perfect way to guarantee no it's robust against errors like "compassion" and "helpfulness", and that's as true of LLMs performing those functions tomorrow as it was of people doing it yesterday.


The people who say "computer says no" are also unaware that's a problem. It's invisible to them. To them the process is the point.

I think that two arent as different as you believe.


Well, possibly. To paraphrase the great American philosopher Donald Rumsfeld - there are known knowns, known unknowns, unknown knowns and unknown unknowns. And making the actual process a black box for the people managing it will create a lot more Unknown Unknowns.


At a former job for a regional bank in South East Asia my boss used to joke that outsourcing is really great for the company, because now they can fail to deliver their software projects for cheaper.


This is not about development. This is about rubber stamping insurance denial by an unaccountable system.


If you sell something in the US, and a customer sues you, going to court and saying you are not accountable because the work was performed by someone in another jurisdiction is not going to go well for you.

The only time that works if you have no assets or presence in the US, or I guess you have an in with the US president.


It is about a.) avoiding criminal liabilities for frauds by the insurance company b.) facilitating desirable fraud by employees while keeping plausible deniality.

It is super hard to build class cast action and suing companies for denied insurance claims is also quite hard - and super expensive. Besides, the current management dont need it to go on forever, they just need it to go on for now. If company gets to pay fine 20 years later and you already pocketed the bonuses and salary, why would you care?


People have a bad intuition about economic mechanisms, but that does not mean that AI won't cause huge regressive effects.

The transition from independent artisans to factory work didn't cause massive unemployment. But it cause the former artisans to lose out, because they no longer had the bargaining power they had before - their work was now a commodity. This resulted in "Engel's pause", a period in which wages stagnated, and so conditions got worse because prices also increased.

But AI also isn't just automation. It's the automation of automation. You may think that you will just level up and learn the new skill set of managing AIs, but the AI companies will be collecting the data to automate that too. Often by watching you.


Judging by the amount of insider interviews it's more than just ads.

Longtime subscriber. Pretty disappointed in how biased their coverage is.

The most critical piece they have put out on AI is oh no it's so powerful it's hacking everything. It's like being in a job interview and saying your biggest weakness is you work too hard.


>Longtime subscriber. Pretty disappointed in how biased their coverage is.

>The most critical piece they have put out on AI is oh no it's so powerful it's hacking everything. It's like being in a job interview and saying your biggest weakness is you work too hard.

What do you think they've missed? Otherwise, all you've demonstrated so far is "their stance on AI doesn't match mine", not that they're "biased". If I was reading HN 5 years ago it would be people saying how economist is biased for or against crypto because the most critical/supportive piece doesn't say it'll go to 0, or will replace all of finance, respectively.


I mean that's a fair take.

But, for me it's not so much that it doesn't match my view. I'm honestly mixed on the whole thing (I am probably most concerned about the finances). It's more that the articles they write seem to align with the eb and flow of anthropics media tempo. This week it's FOMO, next week it's panacea, hack all the things week, followed by mild financial concerns with a but it will be fine tacked at the end. The articles tend to lack concreteness too. Maybe, it's just what reading The Economist is like when it's a domain you actually understand and follow closely?

Honestly, though I could probably say the same for a lot of publications these days.


Also an analogy with the globalization of manufacturing era. People have I think been prone to assuming that the West has a "magic ingredient" which entitles it to revenues from skilled work forever. A presumption that people overseas, especially in the "south" and "east", wouldn't acquire the same skills or culture. The idea that it is so absolutely critical to software development to be in an office in Silicon Valley that it's worth paying enormous premiums even relative to the rest of America and the West (+).

That is being disrupted. Ironically, by American AI firms who want a cut of all software engineering salaries globally.

(+) UK software developer working for an American multinational here, aware that my salary is "great by UK standards but not by American ones"


The WFH aficionados that emerged during Covid had no concept of bargain power or power structures.

Dunno why there was such resistance from the owning class afterwards with return to office mandates.


> The WFH aficionados that emerged during Covid had no concept of bargain power or power structures.

IMO the wrong thing to point at.

How many of us have ever, even before Covid, been in a trade union?

Unions definitely know about bargain power and power structures, yet also get it wrong when new tech arrives.


They should go first tbh, but the system we've allowed them to create mean they'll go last. The same is true of mass redundancies etc. And even when they do go there's golden handshakes/parachutes etc involved. No real skills apart from going to business school and having the right social circle, most of em.


This makes no sense outside of SV.

If you work in the broader corporate world, your heads-down work may typically be writing software, but you're really more like staff IT. You get promoted into some kind of management role like "architect" and end up owning all the implementation instead of just the code.

You get passed the football a lot because that's more effective teamwork. You have weight in meetings because the business is smart enough to realize you are not just writing code. Your maintenance is basically all the operations short of the accounting and client manager stuff for that project.

AI is irrelevant unless you're really feeling a time crunch and have little alternative. Nobody cares how you do it. The meetings are a way bigger deal than the code. These types of devs are the equivalent of a bureaucrat who can sign off on a construction job and then grab a shovel.

This is the actual "future" of dev work... ahem it looks a lot like the past and present for everyone else.


> AI is basically irrelevant unless you're really feeling a time crunch and have little alternative

Which is all of our industry. You're lucky if you're in a pocket outside of timr crunch.


I'm just describing what an actual career looks like beyond the first 5 years of grinding away at a startup and then giving into "the man" or whatever.

I guess it's true that corporate doesn't like hiring junior devs, but I'm not sure it was ever any other way. I'm not seeing where the fire is at. Corporate won't pay you SV wages either, but it's still respectable six-figures. You probably don't get stock either, but everyone gets a management bonus unless they're contractors. This is just basic middle america and it's the vast majority of the workforce.

I'm not trying to piss anyone off when I say this, but all the scifi doomer shit is wildly out of touch and preys on the inexperienced. You should question who is behind it.


I'm clearly not going to convince you with that attitude, but hopefully others reading can benefit from the long view.


fwiw, I was challenging you because your assumptions are not at all what I see around in teams across companies I work with. so was taking the other side and trying to probe further.


Why wouldn't it? The Philippines has a large talent pool of English-speaking workers who can do tons of different IT-related functions that AI can't remotely replace.

If you have a globally distributed sales team with no single office for example with people throughout APAC, the Philippines is the unquestionable place to hire for IT support roles for that region.


POGOs are criminalized and often operated by illegal immigrant Chinese people, it's not really representative. At least that's my understanding having lived in Manila for a few years.


Exactly, that opinion comes straight from parroting international news that have no grasp about what's happening locally there. Most BPO workers are overworked (not all, depend the company, there are thousands of them) but they aren't treated badly.


What does that have to do with the general state of the whole industry? "Scamming" rarely falls into proper "jobs" anyway.


POGOs are not the average BPO/callcenter, and working conditions for most are far better than most jobs, even in scam callcenters (with exceptions, as with anything else).

The average scam callcenter is relatively small scale with 20 workers in it and often is maintained within "family/friends", the POGO industry is very different and it's absolutely not reflecting the reality, that's just a particular niche that is mostly managed by foreign individuals (from China, Cambodia...)


I think offshoring to the Phillipines is extremely net-positive from a purely utilitarian sense

I know a lot of Filipinos and essentially 100% of them in white-collar work are using the money to support their extended families. The money gets spent in a very different way than a Westerner would use it


So why won't they just relocate us en masse to Manila so that a customer from an English locale can speak to someone speaking proper English while I enjoy local pancit, lumpia and stinky tuyo during lunch?


You're only saying this because you're in the fortunate position of not worrying about your job being offshored.


Why does anyone owe you a job if someone elsewhere can do it as good or better and more economically. What entitles you to work simply because you are based in the West?

Sounds like a skill issue


Overall it seems we don't have good intuitions for what kinda work AI 'displaces'. Years of hand-wringing about programmers being put out of a job and instead programmers are the ones paying $200/mo for LLMs

And on the flipside a lot of AI vendor ideas like helping doctors turn voice transcripts into notes has just been annoying for the prospective user--they feel they may as well type it up themselves if they then have to review and correct the AI notes


Outside the English-speaking world, there's generally been a knowledge gap when it comes to programming. Better resources weren't being shared, and AI helps bridge that gap. You could learn the basics, but higher-quality materials were hard to come by. AI actually solves that—so people's reactions depend a lot on their environment

Even learning through open source participation requires understanding the English speaking culture, and that's a kind of knowledge that only people who have lived in those countries can really grasp.

In my case, most of my knowledge came from Microsoft's learning center materials. To actually learn deeply, I had to read papers. And I only knew about them because I went to graduate school. But there were already many libraries that made it easier to apply that knowledge without reading the papers directly.

So I think how useful AI is depends a lot on where you live and what kind of environment you're in

From a recent article in The Economist. It turns out that once again many of the jobs that people predicted would be eliminated by AI have instead received a boost, at least for now. This closely follows another recent report on how Indian BPO firms are surprisingly thriving due to AI.

"Moreover, AI is helping offshore workers in the Philippines do new, more complex jobs. They are picking up work training AI models or supervising AI agents. Hospitals in America are increasingly outsourcing the checking of insurance eligibility and filing of medical records to Filipinos packing AI tools. Mr Gallimore says more “high-value” work, such as accountancy or engineering, is going offshore in part because “AI is a leveller. You can now teach someone complex stuff quickly” and still get it done more cheaply than in America or Europe. Some of this is done at so-called global capability centres, captive back offices that are booming in India and also now growing in the Philippines."

It seems like AI has incidentally commoditized the complement (procedural knowledge), and in turn created greater demand for inputs like human judgement and "empathy".

Do these GCC's have great work life balance? They may be better that the service companies, and may pay better, but WLB is shitty everywhere in India as far as I can tell. As an example, the death of Ernest & Young employee Anna Sebastian sparked a lot of discussion in Indian media since it was attributed to work pressure.[1] Another example I recently heard was a USA Texas based company called CorroHealth suddenly closing shop and laying off 800+ employees in India, the employees allege it was retaliation for asking for overtime payment since they were being made to work till 10 pm.[2]

If you are an American or European with colleagues in India, and if they are working or attending meetings after regular work hours, they don't have good WLB. Given a choice, I doubt they would want to attend the late night meetings. Life in India is already like playing a video game in hard mode, and yet we have to work lot more hours for lot less pay, and be regularly told how shitty offshoring work is.

> but WLB is shitty everywhere in India as far as I can tell

This was what I believed, then I saw how pretty much ALL of my friends at Fortune 100s or 500s and they were amazing. I am sure awful companies exist and the bar for what is good WLB can be lowered by these, but the whole "it is bad everywhere" was simply not true and I felt I had a distorted vision of my Indian friends until I actually visited a lot of them.

My so works at a reinsurance company in one of these GCCs, and her WLB is unmatched. Hours are really flexible. Has a really great manager and team. She even gets to take a day off every month as menstrual leave.

> work lot more hours for lot less pay,

This depends, while the vast majority of roles pay "market rate" there is a strange sweet spot where roles pay a significant amount considering purchasing power and cost of living.

People have a bad intuition about economic mechanisms, but that does not mean that AI won't cause huge regressive effects.

The transition from independent artisans to factory work didn't cause massive unemployment. But it cause the former artisans to lose out, because they no longer had the bargaining power they had before - their work was now a commodity. This resulted in "Engel's pause", a period in which wages stagnated, and so conditions got worse because prices also increased.

But AI also isn't just automation. It's the automation of automation. You may think that you will just level up and learn the new skill set of managing AIs, but the AI companies will be collecting the data to automate that too. Often by watching you.

blocks.html_en:
This makes no sense outside of SV.

If you work in the broader corporate world, your heads-down work may typically be writing software, but you're really more like staff IT. You get promoted into some kind of management role like "architect" and end up owning all the implementation instead of just the code.

You get passed the football a lot because that's more effective teamwork. You have weight in meetings because the business is smart enough to realize you are not just writing code. Your maintenance is basically all the operations short of the accounting and client manager stuff for that project.

AI is irrelevant unless you're really feeling a time crunch and have little alternative. Nobody cares how you do it. The meetings are a way bigger deal than the code. These types of devs are the equivalent of a bureaucrat who can sign off on a construction job and then grab a shovel.

This is the actual "future" of dev work... ahem it looks a lot like the past and present for everyone else.

I'm just describing what an actual career looks like beyond the first 5 years of grinding away at a startup and then giving into "the man" or whatever.

I guess it's true that corporate doesn't like hiring junior devs, but I'm not sure it was ever any other way. I'm not seeing where the fire is at. Corporate won't pay you SV wages either, but it's still respectable six-figures. You probably don't get stock either, but everyone gets a management bonus unless they're contractors. This is just basic middle america and it's the vast majority of the workforce.

I'm not trying to piss anyone off when I say this, but all the scifi doomer shit is wildly out of touch and preys on the inexperienced. You should question who is behind it.

content_html_zh: 来自《经济学人》最近的一篇文章。 事实证明，人们预测将被人工智能取代的许多工作岗位反而得到了提振，至少目前是这样。 紧随其后的是最近另一份关于印度 BPO 公司如何因人工智能而令人惊讶地蓬勃发展的报告。”此外，人工智能正在帮助菲律宾的离岸工人从事新的、更复杂的工作。 他们正在从事训练人工智能模型或监督人工智能代理的工作。 美国的医院越来越多地将保险资格检查和医疗记录归档工作外包给菲律宾人，并配备人工智能工具。 加利莫尔先生表示，更多“高价值”工作，例如会计或工程，正在向海外转移，部分原因是“人工智能是一个平等者。 现在，你可以快速地教别人复杂的东西”，而且仍然比在美国或欧洲更便宜地完成它。 其中一些是在所谓的全球能力中心、专属后台办公室完成的，这些中心在印度蓬勃发展，现在也在菲律宾发展。“人工智能似乎无意中将补充（程序知识）商品化，反过来又对人类判断和“同理心”等投入产生了更大的需求。> 似乎人工智能顺便将补充（程序性知识）商品化了，反过来又对人类判断和“同理心”等输入产生了更大的需求。我认为目前还存在以下问题：人工智能仍然需要操作员，就像推土机需要推土机操作员一样。 就像推土机一样，企业利益相关者总是想挖掘一些东西，现在挖掘速度更快了。“美国的医院越来越多地将保险资格检查和医疗记录归档工作外包给菲律宾人，并配备人工智能工具。 加利莫尔先生说“这个 HIPPA 合规性如何？ 请告诉我，HIPPA 的一个方面要求敏感数据只能由岸上的美国人访问和处理。 你可能会认为，我们为更糟糕的结果支付的医疗保健费用的倍数至少会通过这种基本的后台白领工作来支持我们自己的国内中产阶级这对于 HIPAA 和财务数据来说已经很常见，它通常归结为离岸站点符合合规准则，并且像“洁净室”一样运行，并防止数据泄露。不过，我不认为菲律宾人处理我的数据本质上比美国人更不安全。我最近访问了印度，当我看到有多少公司在那里拥有 GCC 时，我大吃一惊。 许多很酷的办公室、工程和技术角色、良好的工作与生活平衡以及总体上不同的氛围。 事实上，我认识的每一家公司都在那里设有后台办公室。这些海湾合作委员会的工作与生活平衡吗？ 他们可能比服务公司更好，而且支付的费用可能更高，但据我所知，WLB 在印度到处都很糟糕。 例如，安永员工安娜·塞巴斯蒂安（Anna Sebastian）因工作压力而去世，引发了印度媒体的广泛讨论。 [1]我最近听说的另一个例子是，一家位于美国德克萨斯州的公司 CorroHealth 突然关门，并在印度解雇了 800 多名员工，员工声称这是对要求加班费的报复，因为他们被要求工作到晚上 10 点。[2]如果你是美国人或欧洲人，在印度有同事，如果他们在正常工作时间之外工作或参加会议，他们就没有良好的 WLB。 如果有选择的话，我怀疑他们是否愿意参加深夜的会议。 印度的生活已经就像在困难模式下玩电子游戏一样，但我们必须工作更多的时间，工资却少得多，并且经常被告知离岸工作是多么糟糕。[1]https://www.news18.com/viral/26-year-old-ey-pune-employee-su...[2]https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/tamil-nadu/it-employe...> 但据我所知，WLB 在印度到处都很糟糕这是我所相信的，然后我看到我的所有朋友都在财富 100 强或 500 强中，他们都很棒。 我确信存在糟糕的公司，并且这些公司可以降低好的WLB的标准，但是整个“到处都很糟糕”根本不是真的，我觉得我对我的印度朋友的看法是扭曲的，直到我真正拜访了他们中的很多人。我在这些海湾合作委员会之一的一家再保险公司工作，她的WLB是无与伦比的。 时间真的很灵活。 拥有非常出色的经理和团队。 她甚至可以每个月休息一天作为月经假。>工作时间更长，工资却更少，这取决于，虽然绝大多数角色支付“市场价格”，但有一个奇怪的最佳点，考虑到购买力和生活成本，角色支付大量费用。WLB在印度确实很糟糕。 人们在工作中感到紧张和压力，此外糟糕的城市环境也使上下班成为一场噩梦。 我不确定这种情况能持续多久。这确实取决于公司和您的角色。 在印度的 FAANG 中担任高级职位比在当地 WITCH（Wipro Infosys 等）中担任初级职位要好得多，后者因低薪和糟糕的劳工实践而臭名昭著。请不要误会我的意思，FAANG 连印度劳动力的 0.00001% 都不到。 除了FAANG（对亚马逊表示怀疑）之外，几乎所有公司都不好，甚至美国或欧洲的海湾合作委员会似乎也不好。 请注意，我不仅仅考虑 IT——银行、警察似乎都有糟糕的工作文化。在我们变老之前，我们会有良好的公民意识、街道和道路文化吗？ 我只能希望。来自https://theprint.in/opinion/indias-poor-little-rich-people/2...“印度人的生活目的是逃离印度，这可以通过实际离开印度来实现，也可以通过转移到一个封闭的社区来象征性地实现。 一旦印度人逃离印度，印度就成为世界上最好的国家，不需要任何改进”。“通过将自己隔离开来，印度的富人脱离​​了社会。 如果精英不使用公共服务，国家改善公共服务的压力就会较小。”我猜想，当全科医生来访时，他们组织了一些令人畏惧的舞蹈和文化节目，这可能会让全科医生得出结论，这些人生活得很好。他们主要负责全球能力中心的业务流程，并以极低的成本为美国/欧盟公司工作。BPO是指美国公司将业务外包给印度公司。 全球能力中心 (GCC) 意味着它是美国公司在印度的子公司。又名位于其他地点的办公室或部门，其工资低于公司中位数。 想出这些首字母缩写肯定是一项艰苦的工作，我怀疑人工智能是否那么聪明。> 所谓的全球能力中心、专属后台办公室在印度蓬勃发展……我们已经将一些“低成本”工作从印度转移到了其他地区，现在翻译得到了改善......同时，我们正在减少外包工作的比例，因为拥有法学硕士的本地团队能力大大增强...... 如何组织一个较小的高技能团队有很多好处。 即使在 5 年前，我也认为使用当前工具的 10 人团队与 10 名高技能 + 80 名低成本人员的团队相当。是的，矛盾的是，印度软件外包正在增长。 我猜公司的想法是，我们需要对法学硕士所做的所有工作进行某种形式的人工监督，最好向某人支付尽可能少的费用来完成这项工作。不明白为什么这不应该是显而易见的。 如果你有技术可以让昂贵的工人以更便宜的价格做事，为什么同样的技术不能让更便宜的工人做更便宜的事情...... 而且便宜就好...更便宜的价格并不总是会导致需求大幅增加。 只需要这么多的写作和翻译。 因此，降低价格并不意味着花费相同或更多的钱。另一方面，公司以更便宜的价格获得这些服务可能意味着他们提高价格的压力较小。我认为整个杰文悖论都被误用了。 更有效地利用煤炭会带来更多的用例，因为它们变得有利可图。 其中有很多。 对于写作或翻译等许多其他事情，可能没有更多的用例。我认识一位自由翻译，他们的业务比以往任何时候都多，人工智能“大部分”正确在许多企业中还不够好。 你需要监督，最重要的是——以能够打上认可印记的人的形式承担责任。印度科技行业迅速下滑；印度的外包模式已经过时了。我现在可以将可以轻松拆分到低成本地区的任务翻译，而不必处理印度的文化问题。 我还可以快速生成类似（并且不断提高）质量的作品...... 我对法学硕士没有什么用处。我预计印度科技行业会发生严重崩溃，然后一小部分工人才能开始重新建设它。我不确定这是否属实。 我真的希望招聘故事是真实的，但我从现场人员和行业生成的报告中得到的反应并不一致。据我所知，唯一可用的报告是 ICRIER 报告。我还没有阅读该报告本身，但它应该显示出适度的招聘增长。相反，我知道大多数外包供应商在外包技术运营方面都在裁员。>
